In Ps. 103:4 ('qui facit angelos suos spiritus') either accusative can be the object; it is rendered as Gregory's gloss takes it.

nodes.text: 7. We have said that there are nine orders of angels, because, as sacred scripture testifies, we know that there are angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominions, thrones, cherubim and seraphim. For almost every page of sacred scripture testifies that there are angels and archangels. And the books of the prophets, as is well known, often speak of cherubim and seraphim. The apostle Paul, too, lists the names of four orders to the Ephesians, saying: 'Above every principality and power and virtue and dominion' (Eph. 1:21). And again, writing to the Colossians, he says: 'Whether thrones, or powers, or principalities, or dominions' (Col. 1:16). Now he had already described dominions and principalities and powers when speaking to the Ephesians; but when he was about to speak of these to the Colossians as well, he put thrones first, about which he had not yet said anything to the Ephesians. So when thrones are joined to those four which he named to the Ephesians, that is, principalities, powers, virtues and dominions, there are five orders that are expressly named. And when angels and archangels, cherubim and seraphim are added to these, there are found beyond doubt to be nine orders of angels. Hence too it is said through the prophet to that very angel who was created first: 'You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty, in the delights of the paradise of God' (Ezek. 28:12). Here it should be noted that he is said not to have been made to the likeness of God, but to be the seal of likeness, so that the finer the nature in him, the more closely the image of God may be shown to be impressed in him. In that place it is presently added: 'Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz and jasper, chrysolite, onyx and beryl, sapphire, carbuncle and emerald' (ibid. 13). See, he named nine stones, because there are indeed nine orders of angels. That first angel stood adorned and covered with these orders for this reason: because, while he was set above all the hosts of angels, he was the more brilliant by comparison with them.

8. But why have we touched on these choirs of the angels who stood firm by listing them, if we do not also set out their ministries precisely? For in the Greek language angels are called 'messengers', and archangels 'chief messengers'. It should also be known that the word 'angel' is the name of an office, not of a nature. For those holy spirits of the heavenly homeland are indeed always spirits, but they can by no means always be called angels, because they are angels only when something is announced through them. Hence it is said through the Psalmist: 'Who makes spirits his angels' (Ps. 103:4). As if he were saying plainly: he who always has them as spirits also makes them angels when he wills. Those who announce the least things are called angels, and those who announce the highest things archangels. That is why it is not just any angel but the archangel Gabriel who is sent to the Virgin Mary (Luke 1:26). For it was fitting that the highest angel should come for this ministry, since he was announcing the highest of all. They are also given individual names for this reason, so that their names may signify what they are capable of in action as well. For it is not that in that holy city, which full knowledge drawn from the vision of almighty God makes perfect, they are allotted proper names because their persons could not be known without names; but when they come to us to perform some ministry, among us they also take names from their ministries.

9. For Michael means 'Who is like God?', Gabriel 'Strength of God', and Raphael is called 'Medicine of God'. And whenever something of wonderful power is done, Michael is said to be sent, so that from the act itself and from the name it may be understood that no one can do what God has power to do. Hence also that ancient enemy, who through pride desired to be like God, saying: 'I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven, I will sit on the mount of the covenant, on the sides of the north, I will ascend above the height of the clouds, I will be like the Most High' (Isa. 14:13-14), when at the end of the world he is left to his own strength, to be destroyed by the final punishment, is declared to be about to fight with the archangel Michael, as it is said through John: 'A battle was fought with the archangel Michael' (Rev. 12:7), so that he who in pride had raised himself to the likeness of God, being destroyed through Michael, may learn that no one rises to the likeness of God through pride. Gabriel too, who is named the Strength of God, is sent to Mary (Luke 1:26). For he was coming to announce him who deigned to appear humble in order to defeat the powers of the air. Of him it is said through the Psalmist: 'Lift up your gates, you princes, and be lifted up, you eternal gates, and the King of glory shall come in. Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle' (Ps. 23:9-10). And again: 'The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory' (ibid.). So he who, as Lord of hosts and mighty in battle, was coming to make war on the powers of the air had to be announced by the Strength of God. Raphael too is interpreted, as we have said, as the Medicine of God, because, when he touched the eyes of Tobias as if in the office of healing (Tob. 11:13ff.), he wiped away the darkness of his blindness. So it was fitting that the one sent to heal should be called the Medicine of God. But since we have touched on the names of the angels by interpreting them, it now remains for us to go briefly through the terms for their offices themselves.

10. Virtues are indeed the name for those spirits through whom signs and miracles are most often performed. Powers are the name for those who have received this, more powerfully than the others in their order: that the hostile forces are subject to their authority, and are restrained by their power from prevailing to tempt human hearts as much as they wish. Principalities are the name for those who are set over even the good spirits of the angels themselves; while they arrange for those beneath them whatever is to be done, they rule over them for the fulfilling of the divine ministries. Dominions are the name for those who surpass even the powers of the principalities by a lofty difference. For to be a principality is to be first among the rest, but to have dominion is also to possess all who are subject. So those hosts of angels who stand out with wonderful power, because the others are subject to them for obedience, are called dominions. Thrones, too, is the name given to those hosts over whom almighty God always presides to exercise judgement. For since in Latin speech we call thrones 'seats', those are called the thrones of God who are filled with such grace of divinity that the Lord sits in them and through them decrees his judgements. Hence it is said through the Psalmist: 'You sit upon the throne, you who judge equity' (Ps. 9:5). Cherubim, too, means fullness of knowledge. And those more sublime hosts are called cherubim for this reason, that they are filled with a knowledge the more perfect as they contemplate the brightness of God more nearly; so that, within the measure of a creature, they know all things the more fully the nearer they draw, by the merit of their rank, to the vision of their creator. Seraphim, too, is the name for those hosts of holy spirits who, from their singular nearness to their creator, burn with an incomparable love. For seraphim means 'burning' or 'kindling'. Because they are so joined to God that no other spirits come between them and God, they burn the more, the more nearly they see him. Their flame, indeed, is love, because the more finely they gaze upon the brightness of his divinity, the more strongly they blaze in love of him.

12. But, dearest brothers, while I speak, turn back inwardly to yourselves, and examine the merits and thoughts of your inner secrets. See whether you are already doing any good within yourselves; see whether you find the lot of your calling in the number of these hosts which we have briefly touched upon. But woe to the soul that recognises in itself nothing at all of these goods which we have listed; and a worse woe still hangs over it if it both understands that it is deprived of these gifts and does not groan at all. Whoever is such, my brothers, is greatly to be groaned over, because he does not groan. Let us therefore weigh the gifts the elect have received, and with what strength we can, let us pant for the love of so great a lot. Let him who recognises no grace of gifts in himself groan. But let him who recognises lesser gifts in himself not envy others the greater, because those heavenly distinctions of the blessed spirits are so made that some are set above others. Dionysius the Areopagite, an ancient and venerable Father, is reported to say (De Cael. Hier. ch. 7, 9, 13) that it is from the lesser hosts of angels that spirits are sent out, visibly or invisibly, to fulfil a ministry, namely because they come to the comfort of human beings as angels or archangels. For those higher hosts never withdraw from the innermost, since those that are pre-eminent have no use of outward ministry. Against this seems to be what Isaiah says: 'And one of the seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a coal which he had taken with tongs from the altar, and he touched my mouth' (Isa. 6:6-7). But in this saying of the prophet he wants it understood that the spirits who are sent take the name of those whose office they perform. For the angel who carries a coal from the altar to burn away the sins of speech is called seraphim, which means 'burning'. And this sense is believed to be supported, not unfittingly, by what is said through Daniel as well: 'Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him' (Dan. 7:10). For to minister is one thing, to stand before is another, since those minister to God who also go out to us with messages, while those stand before him who so enjoy inward contemplation that they are not sent out at all to carry out outward works.
